title: Breaking the quantum barriers for Graph Collision
abstract: In the graph collision problem, the task is to decide whether a known graph on $n$ vertices contains an edge with both endpoints marked, given query access to the input bits specifying the marked vertices. We first refute the conjectured $Ω(n^{2/3})$ query lower bound with a bounded error quantum algorithm using $\widetilde O(n^{92/139})$ queries. We then refine this approach to obtain a $\widetilde O(n^{11/17})$ query algorithm. We also obtain a $\widetilde O((nq)^{11/17})$ query bound for all (partial) Boolean output functions with positive certificate complexity at most 2 and alphabet size $q$, contrasting a known $Ω(n^{2/3})$ lower bound for such problems with large alphabet sizes. We complement these algorithms with an $Ω(\sqrt{n\log n})$ quantum query lower bound for graph collision, exceeding the $O(\sqrt n)$ certificate complexity barrier for the positive adversary method.

bite.hook: We refute a conjectured n^2/3 quantum query lower bound for graph collision with a new O(n^92/139) query algorithm.
tldr: Addressed the graph collision problem of deciding if a known graph contains an edge with both endpoints marked.
Refuted the conjectured lower bound by building quantum algorithms using refined query complexities.
Complement these algorithms with a quantum query lower bound that exceeds previous complexity barriers.
bite.whyItMatters: Improving quantum algorithm limits for graph problems helps us find the fundamental processing speedups computers can achieve over classical machines.
bite.eli5: Imagine searching a massive social network map for two specific friends who are connected. Researchers found a clever new search shortcut that breaks through what math textbooks said was the absolute speed limit.
